body_markdown:
Lamborghini ushered its entry-level supercar, the Huracán, off the world stage at the end of 2024, doing so with a flurry of searing-hot special editions. Such commemoration was appropriate; the Huracán was superb, combining world-beating performance and friendly road manners. No wonder it won the brand legions of new customers. Can its replacement, the 2026 Lamborghini Temerario, fill those very fine Italian shoes?


Well, it will try, and judging by the spec sheet, with a pyrotechnic flair. Despite remaining relatively approachable—no scissor doors, acre-wide sills, or punishing cabin contortions to deal with here—the Temerario surpasses its predecessor by way of a plug-in hybrid drivetrain that loses two cylinders but gains nearly 300 additional horsepower.


Lamborghini/Lucas Scarfone


At Lamborghini’s invitation, we decamped to[Canadian Tire Motorsports Park](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/the-elsinore-files/tracing-the-colorful-surprising-history-of-canadian-tire-motorsport-park/) to sample the new Temerario. The venue is a 1960s-era Formula 1 track nestled just north of Toronto. It’s virtually impossible on a public road to put a vehicle with 907 horsepower and north of 540 lb-ft of torque through its paces, so the track is essential to fully evaluate machinery whose terminal velocity is higher than a Boeing 787’s take-off speed.


## **Excess Meets** Electricity


[Benjamin Hunting](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/bhunting/)


The Temerario and the Huracán share the same core philosophy: wrapping a welcoming daily driving experience in an extroverted, exotic, high-performance package. (You may recall that the Huracán shared its underpinnings with the Audi R8, another slinky-yet-friendly supercar.) However, the Temerario’s design and engineering path to this common destination could not be more distinct.


[Benjamin Hunting](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/bhunting/)


[Benjamin Hunting](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/bhunting/)


The new Lamborghini jettisons the Huracán’s naturally aspirated V-10 in favor of a twin-turbo 4.0-liter V-8 that leans on a trio of electric motors on its way to an eye-popping dyno result. Two of the e-motors spin the front axles, and they remain in constant operation with no system disconnect, making the Temerario a full-time all-wheel-drive vehicle. The car’s 3.8kWh lithium-ion battery offers up just under 5 miles of electric-only operation, should you require a late-night, non-neighbor-waking creep into your garage bay.


## Specs: 2026 Lamborghini Temerario


**Price:** $382,654 base
**Powertrain:** 4.0-liter V-8 with twin turbochargers and three electric motors; eight-speed dual-clutch transmission
**Output:** 907 hp (engine and e-motors combined); 538 lb-ft (engine), 248 lb-ft (front e-motors) 221 lb-ft (rear e-motor)
**Layout:** Mid-engine, two-door, two-passenger, all-wheel-drive coupe
**Weight:** Approx. 4240 pounds (3725 pounds dry)
**0–60 mph:** 2.7 seconds
**EPA-rated Fuel Economy:** TBD; 16 MPGe combined city/highway, 4.9 miles all-electric range (per Lamborghini)
**Competitors:**[Ferrari 296 GTB](https://www.hagerty.com/media/new-car-reviews/first-look-review-2022-ferrari-296-gtb/) ,[McLaren Artura](https://www.hagerty.com/media/new-car-reviews/2023-mclaren-artura-review-familiar-face-fresh-guts/)


Lest you think Lamborghini relies primarily on its electrified tech to shock and awe with the pedal flat, consider that its boosted and mid-mounted flat-plane-crank V-8 delivers 789 of the total 907 horses, redlining at an adrenaline-inducing 10,000 rpm. Think superbike packed into a gentrified cabin, requiring drivers to expertly exercise fast-twitch muscles when paddle-shifting through the eight-speed dual-clutch transmission’s gears.


[Benjamin Hunting](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/bhunting/)


[Benjamin Hunting](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/bhunting/)


[Benjamin Hunting](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/bhunting/)


[Benjamin Hunting](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/bhunting/)


Lamborghini claims that the coupe’s body shape—a clean-sheet design sitting on the automaker’s new electrified platform that shares some elements with the larger Revuelto—offers 103% more rear downforce and 30% better cooling as compared to the[Huracán Evo](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/the-elsinore-files/the-perfect-modern-lamborghini-is-the-cheapest-one/) . Step up to the Alleggerita lightweight package, and that aero-driven stick climbs another 67%, along with a 64-pound weight savings over the base car, and much grippier track-specific Bridgestone Potenza Race tires at all four corners.


## **Taking Off in the Temerario**


[Benjamin Hunting](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/bhunting/)


Lamborghini/Lucas Scarfone


Sitting in pit lane at CTMP, two thoughts dominated as we waited in the Temerario’s left seat for the go-signal from the lead driver.


First: how Lamborghini’s software systems would keep the hybrid setup at peak performance when pushed to the limit. My test car’s handling and drivetrain modes were set to Corsa (one of 13 different “driving experiences” programmed into the car), with its hybrid system tuned for maximum track attack. As with so many modern marvels of automotive engineering packed with electronic assistance, we weren’t sure to what extent the Lamborghini would feel like it was driving *for* rather than entrusting control *to* the driver at the limit.


Lamborghini/Lucas Scarfone


Second: the nature of the track itself. Canadian Tire Motorsports Park stretches across nearly 2.5 miles of asphalt, with nearly every turn—save the multi-segment Moss Corner—capable of supporting high-speed entry. The track’s most complex set of apexes leads into one of the longest back straights in North America, comparable to both Road Atlanta and Road America in showcasing the tenacity of high-performance vehicles. Before heading into a gradual, curving braking zone, it promised to tease the Temerario’s 215 mph top speed.


## Hybrid Co-Conspirator


Lamborghini/Lucas Scarfone


Halfway through the out-lap in the standard-issue Temerario, we realized Lamborghini made sure drivers would feel connected to the car on track. There is a lot going on in the coupe’s cockpit in a closed circuit setting, ranging from the stentorian roar of its V-8 at 10,000 rpm directly behind your head, to the insistent flash of the gauge cluster’s digital tachometer directing you to snap the upshift paddle to keep the car’s titanium conrods on pace for the next run through the revs. The drivetrain is suprisingly visceral, though not for lack of electric sophistication: When the car senses wheelspin or yaw beyond set parameters, rather than completely cut the engine’s power delivery, the software will divert engine output to charge the battery. The effect is to keep pistons pumping, ready to go, while the front e-motors take over and pull the car back into shape. All of the above occurs in the blink of an eye, and with such smooth self-correction that it feels part and parcel of the natural action to counter-steer when negotiating a slide.


[Benjamin Hunting](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/bhunting/)


For such a large and heavy (hovering around 4000 pounds) vehicle, the Lamborghini is communicative as to what’s happening under its standard Bridgestone Pontenza Sport tires (20 inches up front, 21-inches at the rear). This is especially true under braking, where the Temerario exhibits a surprising but controllable tendency to move side-to-side while shedding heat and energy at the end of CTMP’s long straight. Just how rapidly were we traveling before caving to better angels applying the Temerario’s 10-piston front stoppers? Hard to say exactly, as we were paying much more attention to keeping the car within the width of the racing surface rather than eyeing its gauges. But while glancing at the tachometer, we saw 176 mph displayed beneath it, just prior to *upshifting* at redline.


Lamborghini/Lucas Scarfone


After spending half the morning behind the wheel of the street-focused Temerario, we swapped into the Alleggerita edition. This version transforms with the addition of Potenza Race rubber and downforce, especially on a fast track like CTMP. So much quicker were the car’s corner exits that we struggled to keep up with the twin-turbo V-8’s shift points, which came that much sooner and at a different rhythm than they had earlier in the day. And that braking wiggle? All gone, thanks in large part to the additional mechanical grip afforded by the more aggressive tires.


## **Electrification Done Right**


[Benjamin Hunting](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/bhunting/)


Electrification is almost inescapable among supercars in the $382,000 range, where the Temerario’s window sticker starts. (Think McLaren Artura and Ferrari 296 GTB.) Though some argue the weight penalty and blunt-force torque delivery that batteries and motors bring have dulled the thrill of once-analog supercars, this car suggests otherwise. The electric motors course-correct when needed, bolstering the soaring internal combustion power curve but never overshadowing it. The Temerario’s engaging antics, when driven as intended in an environment that rewards aero stick and a horizontal throttle, prove that even Lamborghini’s entry-level bull is rambunctious.


Yes, the Temerario is fast. Yes, it makes all the right noises. And yes, its hunched wedge profile is classic Lamborghini. But what’s most important is the genuine fun one experiences when driving it, even in the upper reaches of its envelope, when there’s a dose of terror in the mix. It’s this successful pursuit of exhilaration, this injection of emotion in between the fiery explosions of its V-8 and the propulsion of its e-motors, that make the Temerario so appealing. Most anyone who loves driving could try this Lamborghini on for size and find it a perfect fit.


## 2026 Lamborghini Temerario


**Highs:** Operatic V-8 song; Saturn V levels of forward thrust; comfortable cabin and friendly demeanor; traffic-stopping looks.


**Lows:** Heavier and more complex than the Huracán it replaces; EV range could be improved.


**Takeaway:** Supercars should feel super, and the Temerario does. It blends the brute force of electric power with the fire-spitting emotion of an Italian V-8, all in a package that is surprisingly approachable.
